title: Ang 1043–1070: Amar Das's Solhe
hookLine: the third Guru's long Maru hymns
tomorrow: what do you say when someone mocks you to your face?

cards: You stand up to present. The room goes quiet, chairs creak, and every face turns your way. Then your mind does a strange thing: it turns around too, and starts staring at you.
How do I sound? What are they thinking? Is my voice shaking?
And that's the moment the words vanish. Freezing isn't about the audience. It's about which way you're facing.
The third Guru, Guru Amar Das, wrote long Maru hymns that keep coming back to exactly that question.

teach.b: From ang 1043, these pages hold Guru Amar Das's Solhe, the third Guru's turn at the long sixteen-stanza form Guru Nanak used. Two words run through them, and they're both about faces. Mukh means face.
A gurmukh is someone turned toward the Guru: facing the teaching, the Word, the One.
A manmukh is someone turned toward their own mind, its moods and its noise.
Again and again in these hymns, the gurmukh is steady and the manmukh is tossed around, not because one is good and one is wicked, but because of where each is looking.
Turned toward your own mind, everything is about you: your voice, your nerves, your score. Turned toward the Guru, there's something bigger to look at, and the self gets quieter.
That's why this is useful on an ordinary day. In the bright room, the cure for freezing isn't to stop caring.

teach.h: TURN TO WHAT YOU CAME TO GIVE.
teach.b: It's to turn: from what they think of me to what I came here to give. Same room, same faces, a different direction.
The third Guru's Solhe keep asking, page after page, where are you facing?

how: Guru Amar Das's Maru Solhe are sung in kirtan and read in order in a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; the words gurmukh and manmukh are part of everyday Sikh vocabulary.

o: where Guru Ram Das's ballad in Maru begins
where Guru Nanak's twelve-month song starts
where Guru Amar Das's long Maru hymns begin

games.q: which way are you facing — tap the pairs.
p: the third Guru, writing Solhe in Maru

s: gurmukh simply means someone who can read Gurmukhi script
in these hymns it's someone turned toward the Guru: a direction, not a reading skill.
in the hymns, the difference between gurmukh and manmukh is where each is facing
toward the Guru, or toward one's own mind and its noise.
Guru Amar Das invented the Solhe form
it's the long form Guru Nanak used; these pages are the third Guru's turn at it.

games.q: at a cousin's wedding someone hands you the mic for a surprise toast. your mind starts staring at you. by the third Guru's picture, what steadies you?
o: turning from what they think of me to what I'm here to give.
reading each guest's face first to see if they approve.
handing the mic back; steady people don't speak off the cuff.
games.why: the gurmukh is steady because of where they're looking. turned toward something bigger than yourself, the self gets quieter.

practice: Sit up tall, chin level, and let your face settle as if someone kind were sitting right across from you. Each time your attention turns back to how you look or sound, gently turn it forward again, toward that kind face.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1043. Where Guru Amar Das's Maru Solhe begin, with their steady question: gurmukh or manmukh, which way are you facing?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gurmukh, one turned toward the Guru; mukh is a face. Its pair is manmukh (ਮਨਮੁਖਿ).

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the third's solhe, and the turn from what they think of me to what I came to give. Day fifteen-seventy-three, facing forward.
